title: Channa and Kanthaka
hookLine: the charioteer and the white horse ride out at midnight through the city gate
last: NEKKHAMMA — THE HARDEST LEAVING IS QUIET.

lines: WHO DROVE YOU TO THE AIRPORT?
cards: Who drove you to the airport the first time you really left home? Who sat in the waiting room with you, or carried the boxes up three flights of stairs?
Most big journeys have someone at the very start, someone who doesn't come all the way but gets you out the door. The prince has two. It's midnight, and the palace is asleep.
In the stable courtyard, his charioteer, Channa, holds the reins of a great white horse named Kanthaka.
The prince swings up into the saddle, Channa takes hold of the horse's tail, and the three of them head for the city gate.

teach.h: BORN ON THE SAME DAY AS HIM.
teach.b: The later telling makes this ride glow. Kanthaka is enormous and pure white, and the tradition says both he and Channa were born on the very same day as the prince.
No hired driver, no borrowed horse: these are the companions of his whole life. The gods, the telling says, muffled the sound of Kanthaka's hooves with their hands so no one would wake.
The city gate, so heavy it took many men to open, swung open by itself.
And at the gate a figure appears in the air: Mara, the tempter. Turn back, he says. In seven days you'll be king of the whole world.
The prince doesn't even slow down. Mara is patient, and he'll be back in this story. But tonight the three ride on, and by dawn, the telling says, they've crossed three kingdoms.
Whatever you make of muffled hooves and opening gates, the heart of the scene is simple and human.
The prince did not leave alone. Channa, who answered his questions honestly on the road to the park, now helps him go, knowing it means losing him. Kanthaka carries him as far as a horse can.
Every tradition of the story keeps them, and Buddhists remember them with real affection. Great journeys are often told as solo adventures.
This one, the most well-known departure in Buddhism, begins with a friend holding a horse's tail in the dark.

how: Temple murals and carvings across the Buddhist world show the great departure, the prince on the white horse Kanthaka with Channa holding its tail, and some festivals reenact the ride.

o: the white horse that carried the prince away
the palace stable where the horses slept
the king's war elephant, kept for battle

games.q: who's on the midnight ride — tap the pairs.

s: in the telling, Channa and Kanthaka were born the same day as the prince
lifelong companions, not a hired driver and a borrowed horse.
the prince slipped out of the city alone
Channa and Kanthaka rode with him through the gate.
Mara offered to make him king of the world
in seven days, if he turned back. he didn't slow down.

games.q: at the city gate, a voice in the air says: turn back, and in seven days you'll rule the world. what do you do?
o: turn back and take the throne.
games.why: he rides on. Mara, the tempter, will be back, but tonight the three cross three kingdoms by dawn.

practice: Think of someone who got you somewhere: a parent who drove you to your first job, a friend who talked you into applying, a teacher who opened a door, a stranger who gave you directions when you were lost.
Picture their face and the moment, the car, the room, the road. Then, silently or out loud, say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Kanthaka. The white horse, born the same day as the prince, who carried him out of the palace at midnight, with Channa holding his tail.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the prince's white horse.

carryVoice: Your line: someone rode with you. Two companions, one gate, and a long night's ride. Day thirty-eight, done.
